442.title: Job, a good man (Job 1–2)
442.hook: a good man loses everything, and still does not curse God
442.carry: the lord gave, the lord took
442.howItsDone: Christians often read the book of Job in times of grief and suffering, and Job's words "the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away" are said at many Christian funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five books of the Psalms. Your line: every feeling has a psalm. Today, the hardest book of wisdom.

"There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job." It opens like a folk tale: once upon a time, far away. Nobody knows for sure where Uz was, and the book never says Job was an Israelite. He's just a man, somewhere east, with seven sons, three daughters, thousands of sheep and camels, and a habit of getting up early to offer sacrifices in case his children had sinned at their parties. Then, in a single day, four messengers arrive. Raiders took the oxen. Fire fell on the sheep. Raiders took the camels. And the last: a great wind hit the house where his children were eating, and they are all dead.
screen: `A MAN IN THE LAND OF UZ.` → `FOUR MESSENGERS, ONE DAY.` → `EVERYTHING GONE.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible calls Job "perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil." Perfect here means whole, blameless, not flawless. First, the reader sees what Job never does: a scene in heaven. The heavenly beings come before God, and among them is one called, in Hebrew, ha-satan. The satan, with the word the in front, more a job title than a name: the adversary, the accuser. Christian tradition has identified him with the devil; some scholars read him here as a member of the heavenly court whose role is to accuse. God points out Job, and the accuser asks the question the whole book turns on: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" Is anyone good for free, or only for the reward? Take it all away, and see. So it is taken. Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground and worships: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Then his own body is struck with sores, and he sits in ashes, scraping himself with broken pottery. His wife, who has also just lost ten children, says: curse God, and die. Job answers: "shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?" The reader knows about the heavenly scene; Job never finds out. He lives through all of it without the explanation.

443.title: Seven days of silence (Job 2:11–13)
443.hook: his friends sit with him for a week without speaking; that's the best thing they do
443.howItsDone: Christians practice a ministry of presence by visiting the sick and the grieving, staying at wakes and sitting with the dying; many pastors and hospital chaplains point to Job's friends' silent week as a model.

The funeral home. The hospital corridor. The kitchen of a friend whose marriage just ended. Someone walks in with a casserole or a card, mind racing for the right thing to say, and everything sounds wrong. They're in a better place. It'll get easier. Everything happens for a reason. A mouth opens, and closes again. The silence is hard to bear, and it's tempting to fill it with something. Three men in the book of Job, at least at first, did something braver. They said nothing at all. For a week.
screen: `THE HOSPITAL CORRIDOR.` → `RACING FOR THE RIGHT WORDS.` → `THREE MEN SAY NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible: "Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him." They made an appointment. They coordinated, traveled from three different places, and arrived together, on purpose. Then they see him from a distance and don't recognize him; disease and grief have changed him that much. They weep aloud, tear their robes, and throw dust into the air over their heads, the signs of mourning. And then: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." On the ground, in the ash, at his level. Seven days of mourning appears elsewhere in the Bible too: Joseph mourned his father Jacob for seven days. Jews still keep that week of sitting with mourners, called shiva, from the Hebrew for seven. Then a quiet detail: the friends don't speak until Job speaks first. They follow his lead. The sad part, as the next days will show, is that once they open their mouths, it goes badly. Some readers say the week of silence was the best comfort they gave. Paul's letter to the Romans puts the same instinct simply: "weep with them that weep."

444.title: Let the day perish (Job 3)
444.hook: Job curses the day he was born, and the Bible keeps his words
444.howItsDone: Many Christians pray laments, honest complaints brought to God, using the words of Job, the psalms of lament and Lamentations, and some churches hold services of lament after tragedies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three friends sat on the ground with Job, saying nothing. Your line: they sat with him.

People say it when someone puts up with a lot: she has the patience of Job. The phrase comes from the letter of James, and it paints a man who suffers quietly, never raising his voice. Hold that picture. Because after seven days of silence on the ground, Job finally speaks. And the first thing out of his mouth, the opening of the long poem at the heart of the book, isn't patient. It isn't quiet. It's a curse.
screen: `THE PATIENCE OF JOB.` → `SEVEN DAYS OF SILENCE END.` → `NOT WHAT ANYONE EXPECTS.`

segments.voice: Chapter three begins, in the King James Bible: "After this opened Job his mouth, and cursed his day." Not God. His day, the day he was born. "Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived." He wants that day erased, the stars of that night dark, the dawn never to come. Then the questions: "Why died I not from the womb?" Why is light given to someone in misery? And: "For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me." Here's the striking thing about the book's shape. Chapters one and two are prose, like a story. Right here, with this curse, the book switches to poetry, and stays poetry until the last page. The pain gets the poetry. And the Bible keeps every word; it doesn't cut this chapter or soften it. The prophet Jeremiah says something close: cursed be the day wherein I was born. Two people of faith saying the unsayable, and scripture keeps both. Now back to James. The Greek word translated patience there is hupomone, which the lexicons give as endurance or steadfastness: holding on under a weight without walking away. That fits Job better than quiet ever did. Job never stops talking to God, even when he's shouting. Christians have often called this kind of speech lament: prayer that tells God the truth about how bad it is. On this reading, even a curse on your birthday, said to God, is still a way of staying in the conversation.
screen: `HE CURSES HIS DAY, NOT GOD` · `FROM PROSE INTO POETRY` · `THE BIBLE KEEPS EVERY WORD` · `PATIENCE MEANS ENDURANCE` · then, large: `LET THE DAY PERISH WHEREIN I WAS BORN.`

445.title: Bad comfort (Job 4–5)
445.hook: his friends insist he must have sinned; they're wrong
445.tomorrow: I know that my redeemer lives
445.howItsDone: Christian pastors and chaplains often study Job's friends as a warning in pastoral care training: listen first, and do not tell sufferers their pain is a punishment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job cursing the day he was born, and the Bible keeping every word. Your line: even this is prayer.

Everything happens for a reason. God doesn't give you more than you can handle. Maybe this is a wake-up call. At least you're young. Most of us have heard sentences like these at the worst moment of our lives, or, if we're honest, said them. They're usually meant kindly, by people who love us and can't stand the silence. And they can land like a slap. The book of Job has a name for the people who say them, coined by Job himself. But first, the man who speaks right after Job's curse: Eliphaz, the gentlest of the three.
screen: `EVERYTHING HAPPENS FOR A REASON.` → `MEANT KINDLY.` → `LANDS LIKE A SLAP.`

segments.voice: Eliphaz begins politely, almost apologetically: if we try to talk with you, will you be upset? He reminds Job that Job has comforted others in his time. Fair enough. Then the turn, in the King James Bible: "Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?" Innocent people don't get destroyed. "Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same." You reap what you sow; do the math. He even describes a frightening night vision to back himself up: "Then a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up." And he has lines that sound like they belong on a wall: "Yet man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward." Here's the strange part. A lot of what Eliphaz says is true somewhere. The apostle Paul even quotes him, in First Corinthians, as scripture. The problem isn't the sayings. It's where he points them: a general rule fitted onto a grieving man the reader knows is blameless. He explains Job's pain to Job. Job's reply comes a few chapters later: "miserable comforters are ye all." Centuries later, in John's Gospel, the disciples see a man born blind and ask Jesus: who sinned, this man, or his parents? Jesus answers: neither. And at the very end of Job, God himself will say these friends got it wrong. They came to comfort. They sat in silence beautifully. Then they started explaining.

446.title: I know that my redeemer lives (Job 19:25–27)
446.hook: in the depths, Job reaches for hope anyway
446.howItsDone: Job 19:25 stands among the opening sentences of the Anglican burial service as a confession of hope in the resurrection, and it is sung as the soprano aria "I know that my Redeemer liveth" in Handel's Messiah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eliphaz and the comfort that hurt. Your line: don't explain their pain.

By chapter nineteen, it's bad. The friends have stopped being gentle. Job says his brothers keep their distance, his servants ignore him, his breath is strange to his own wife, and little children mock him when he stands up. "Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me." Nobody does. Then he wishes for something odd: that his words could be carved with an iron pen into rock, filled in with lead, so someone someday would know what he said. His wish came true. What he says next is still read aloud and sung.
screen: `FRIENDS GONE, FAMILY DISTANT.` → `CARVE MY WORDS IN ROCK.` → `THE WISH CAME TRUE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth." The Hebrew word for redeemer is go'el, and it's a family word before it's a church word. A go'el was your nearest relative with a duty to you. If debt forced you to sell your land, your go'el bought it back. If you were sold into slavery, your go'el paid to free you. If you were killed, your go'el made sure your blood didn't go unanswered. In the book of Ruth, Boaz is the go'el who buys back a family's land and marries the widow Ruth. So when Job, abandoned by family and friends, says my go'el lives, he's saying: somebody is still on my side, and will stand up for me at the end, even if nobody here will. Who is it? Readers have heard it differently. Christian tradition hears Christ: the redeemer who lives and stands on the earth at the last day. Handel set it to music in Messiah, and the Book of Common Prayer sets it among the sentences that open its burial service. Jewish commentators have heard God himself as Job's defender. Some scholars think Job meant a heavenly witness, the advocate he mentions a few chapters earlier. And the next verse is hard to translate: in my flesh shall I see God, or without my flesh. The King James chose "yet in my flesh shall I see God." Either way, a man at the bottom reaches up anyway.

447.title: Where is wisdom? (Job 28)
447.hook: men mine for silver and gold, but wisdom isn't found in the earth
447.carry: the fear of the lord is wisdom
447.howItsDone: Many Christians pray for wisdom before decisions and study, and some read Job 28 as a meditation on the limits of what human cleverness can dig out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job carving a hope in rock. Your word was redeemer, and your line: my redeemer lives.

Chapter twenty-eight of Job begins underground. The arguing suddenly stops, and a poem starts, about miners. They push back the darkness. They cut shafts in places no traveler goes. They hang on ropes, swinging, far from other people. They turn mountains over by the roots and find sapphires in the stone and gold in the dust. No bird knows these paths; no vulture's eye has seen them; no lion has walked them. Humans, the poem says, can dig their way to almost anything. Almost.
screen: `SHAFTS CUT INTO ROCK.` → `MINERS ON ROPES.` → `HUMANS CAN REACH ALMOST ANYTHING.`

segments.voice: The poem opens, in the King James Bible: "Surely there is a vein for the silver, and a place for gold where they fine it." Silver has a place. Gold has a place. Then the question: "But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?" You can dig, but "The depth saith, It is not in me: and the sea saith, It is not with me." You can't buy it either. The poem piles up gold, onyx, sapphire, coral, pearls and topaz, and sets them all aside: "the price of wisdom is above rubies." Even death and destruction say they've only heard rumors of it. So where is it? "God understandeth the way thereof, and he knoweth the place thereof." Then the last verse, in which God speaks to humankind: "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding." The Hebrew word is yirah. It can mean fear, and it can mean awe and reverence, standing in front of something far greater than you; readers often hear the second here. Notice what the poem is doing. Job and his friends have spent chapter after chapter trying to work out exactly why he's suffering, each sure he has the answer. This poem quietly says: nobody can dig that out. Wisdom isn't a fact you extract. It starts with awe, and with turning away from harm. Scholars debate who speaks the poem, Job or the book's narrator; it reads like a breath in the argument. And it sounds a theme you'll hear again when Proverbs opens.
screen: `A VEIN FOR THE SILVER` · `THE DEPTH SAITH, IT IS NOT IN ME` · `ABOVE RUBIES` · `GOD KNOWETH THE PLACE` · then, large: `THE FEAR OF THE LORD, THAT IS WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Picture a conversation you'll have soon, at work, at home or on the phone, and notice where you usually rush, argue or try to win. Now picture going in with a little awe, listening for what you don't already know, the way a miner looks for a vein. If you pray, ask for wisdom, perhaps with the poem's last line; if not, simply set that intention.

448.title: The whirlwind (Job 38–39)
448.hook: God answers with questions: where were you when I laid the earth's foundations?
448.howItsDone: Christians often read God's speeches from the whirlwind in times of suffering and at services celebrating creation, and some find in them a call to humility and wonder rather than an explanation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, miners in the dark and wisdom no treasure can buy. Your line: the fear of the Lord is wisdom.
screen: `THE FEAR OF THE LORD IS WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Since chapter three, people have talked about God. The friends explained him. Job accused him, pleaded with him, demanded a hearing, like a man filing a complaint in court: oh that one would hear me, let the Almighty answer me. Then a young man named Elihu bursts in and talks for chapters more. And then the sky changes. The wind picks up. Dust spins. And for the first time since the opening scenes in heaven, God speaks. Not to the friends. To Job. Out of a storm.
screen: `CHAPTER AFTER CHAPTER OF TALK.` → `LET THE ALMIGHTY ANSWER ME.` → `THE SKY CHANGES.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind, and said, Who is this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge?" And God doesn't answer Job's questions. He asks his own. "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding." Who set its measurements? Who laid its cornerstone, "When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?" Who shut the sea behind doors and told it, "Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed"? Have you walked the springs of the deep, seen the storehouses of the snow? "Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?" Then chapter thirty-nine turns to wild animals: lions hunting, mountain goats giving birth where no one sees, the wild donkey scorning the crowds of the city, the ostrich that leaves her eggs in the sand and still scorns the horse and its rider, and the war horse: "hast thou clothed his neck with thunder?" Here's what's strange. God never mentions the scene in heaven, never explains the test. Job never finds out why. Instead, he's taken on a tour of a universe that is huge, wild and mostly not about humans at all. Readers hear this differently. Some hear a rebuke: who are you to question me? Some hear wonder, God sharing his delight in creation with a man who's only been staring at his own ashes. Some find it unsatisfying, and the book lets them. But one thing is plain. Job asked God to answer. God came.
screen: `ANSWERED OUT OF THE WHIRLWIND` · `WHEN THE MORNING STARS SANG` · `PLEIADES, ORION, THE WILD GOAT` · `NO EXPLANATION, BUT GOD CAME` · then, large: `WHERE WAST THOU WHEN I LAID THE FOUNDATIONS OF THE EARTH?`

segments.voice: Look at something wild and huge: the sky, clouds stacked high, a big old tree, or the farthest window if you're indoors. Let your problems sit in proportion, not erased, just smaller against the sky. If you pray, let the question rest in you: where were you? If not, let wonder have the time.
The whirlwind. The storm God speaks from at the end of Job, answering with questions about the stars, the sea and the wild animals.
Your line: where were you? The week walked with Job: a good man, shiva, hupomone, bad comfort, my redeemer, where is wisdom, the whirlwind. A hard week, and you stayed.
